results.result: The study recruited 18 pharmacoresistant epilepsy patients (10 females, mean age 30 years) who were French native speakers with intact language functions and normal hearing. Patients listened to ~10 minutes each of natural speech and instrumental music while undergoing whole-brain intracranial EEG recordings, yielding 271 electrodes and 3371 contacts across the cohort.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C76-C87 provide comprehensive demographic, clinical, and methodological details about the study participants and experimental design. The information is internally consistent and appropriately detailed for a neurophysiological study, with proper ethical approval documented (C80, C81).

results.result: The majority (~70%) of focal and network-level neural activity is shared between speech and music processing across frequency bands. Preferred responses account for 3-15% and selective responses for 6-30% depending on frequency band, with selectivity more prominent in lower frequencies and marginal in high-frequency activity (6-12%).
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C16-C20, C22, C40-C43, C69 collectively demonstrate the predominance of shared neural responses through multiple complementary analyses (spectral power and connectivity). The quantitative findings are consistent across different analytical approaches and are supported by Figures 2, 3, and 8, providing converging evidence for this major conclusion.

results.result: There is an absence of anatomical regional selectivity for speech and music processing. No single cortical region shows exclusive selectivity to either domain, and population prevalence analyses reveal that the majority of patients show shared responses at the regional level in every cortical region examined.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C48, C49, C56, C72 are supported by population prevalence analyses (Figures 5, 6, 10) showing that no anatomical region is exclusively selective to speech or music. The finding that 10 minutes of instrumental music activated regions classically labeled as speech-selective (C56) provides strong evidence against anatomical regional selectivity.

results.result: Domain-selective neural responses are restricted to distributed and frequency-specific coherent oscillations rather than anatomical regions. When considering the entire frequency spectrum, selectivity drops ~4-fold compared to single frequency bands, and cross-frequency selectivity in connectivity is near zero except in the delta range (speech=0.19%, music=0.06%).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C25-C27, C44-C47, C57, C62, C73 demonstrate that selectivity exists only at the level of frequency-specific distributed networks, not anatomical regions. The cross-frequency analysis (Figure 4, 9) provides strong quantitative evidence that selectivity is frequency-specific and marginal when considering the full spectrum, supporting the concept of spectral fingerprints.

results.result: Speech and music show complementary activation/deactivation patterns across frequency bands: for low frequencies (<15 Hz), speech selective responses were mostly deactivations and music responses were activations compared to baseline, with this pattern reversing for high frequencies (>15 Hz).
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 describe a specific pattern observed in Figures 2 and 3. This complementary pattern across frequency bands is clearly documented and provides insight into the frequency-specific nature of neural responses to speech versus music.

results.result: Low-frequency (1-9 Hz) neural activity encoding acoustic peakRates captures significantly more channels than high-frequency amplitude (t=13.39, q<0.0001). This encoding occurs throughout the cortex extending beyond auditory regions to motor and frontal areas, with the best encoding in primary auditory cortex showing similar TRF shapes and prediction accuracy (r up to 0.55) for both speech and music.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C37, C65-C68 present a comprehensive TRF analysis with strong statistical support (Figure 7). The finding that low-frequency activity better encodes acoustic features than high-frequency amplitude is well-supported by statistical comparisons and consistent spatial patterns. The similar encoding for speech and music further supports the shared processing conclusion.

results.result: During speech or music perception, the auditory cortex is mostly connected to the rest of the brain through slow neural dynamics, with ~33% of channels showing significant coherence at delta rate compared to only ~12% at high-frequency activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 are supported by seed-based connectivity analysis (Figure 8) showing clear quantitative differences in connectivity strength across frequency bands. This finding complements the TRF results and reinforces the importance of low-frequency dynamics in auditory processing.

results.result: The left hemisphere appears to be more strongly involved in speech and music processing, but this result is biased by the inclusion of a majority of patients with left hemisphere exploration.
results.evaluation: Claim C21 appropriately acknowledges a sampling bias in the study. The authors correctly note this limitation and provide evidence (C22, C35) that patterns remain similar across hemispheres when analyzed separately, demonstrating appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: Data preprocessing included bipolar re-referencing to increase spatial sensitivity, removal of 3% of channels located outside the brain, artifact rejection of 18% of channels on average, and rejection of 6% of speech epochs and 7% of music epochs. Six canonical frequency bands were analyzed: delta (1-4 Hz), theta (5-8 Hz), alpha (8-12 Hz), beta (18-30 Hz), low-gamma (30-50 Hz), and HFa (80-120 Hz).
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C92 describe standard preprocessing procedures for intracranial EEG data. The methods are appropriate and well-documented, with reasonable artifact rejection rates. The choice of frequency bands is conventional and well-justified by the cited literature.

results.result: The study proposes that domain-selective brain regions should be considered as functionally homogeneous but spatially distributed voxels rather than anatomical landmarks, and demonstrates the value of considering shared, preferred, and selective responses across activation/deactivation patterns, frequency bands, and both power and connectivity analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C70-C71, C74-C75 present methodological and conceptual conclusions drawn from the study's findings. These interpretations are well-supported by the data and offer a framework for reconciling apparently contradictory findings in the literature. The tripartite classification (shared/preferred/selective) is a valuable contribution.

results.result: The literature shows mixed evidence regarding selectivity versus shared processing for speech and music, with some studies claiming distinct brain regions for language versus other processes while others suggest shared neural substrates. Previous work has established that speech unfolds faster than music, that different frequency bands serve different cognitive functions, and that ecological stimuli elicit more distributed neural responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C15, C50-C55, C59-C60, C63 accurately summarize relevant prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims provide necessary context for the current study and are appropriately attributed to cited sources. The characterization of mixed evidence in the literature is fair and well-documented.

results.result: The study acknowledges that activations and deactivations can co-occur in the same spatial location across different frequency bands, and that the analytical approach extending over a long period does not allow direct isolation of specific brain operations.
results.evaluation: Claims C61 and C64 appropriately acknowledge methodological considerations and limitations. The recognition that the temporal integration approach cannot isolate specific operations is an important caveat that demonstrates scientific rigor and appropriate interpretation of the results.

results.result: The study found that approximately 70% of neural responses are shared between speech and music processing across frequency bands, with selective responses more present in lower frequency bands (~30% up to alpha) and marginal in high-frequency activity (6-12%). Speech and music showed complementary activation/deactivation patterns across frequencies.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. The editor states the study 'demonstrates that speech and music largely share network-level brain activities,' and Reviewer 3 notes the manuscript provides 'compelling and clear evidence towards shared neural signatures for speech and music.' Reviewer 1 acknowledges 'a significant portion of both focal and network-level brain activity is commonly shared.'

results.result: The study reports an absence of anatomical regional selectivity for speech and music processing, finding that no single cortical region is solely selective to speech or music, and that 10 minutes of instrumental music activated regions classically labeled as speech-selective.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge this finding, they raise significant concerns about its interpretation. Reviewer 1 notes the 'concept of selectivity may not present sufficient theoretical accuracy' and that 'the mere presence of significant differences...does not present a strong case that a region is specifically selective.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes that the study 'cannot definitively rule out the possibility of distinct, non-overlapping neural representations at the microscale' and that each electrode records from thousands of neurons, potentially masking finer-grained selectivity.

results.result: Domain-selective neural responses are restricted to distributed and frequency-specific coherent oscillations. When considering the entire frequency spectrum, selectivity drops approximately 4-fold compared to single frequency bands, and selectivity is only visible at the level of frequency-specific distributed networks.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently support this finding. Reviewer 3 states the study 'provides evidence for a low level of selectivity across spectral signatures' and praises 'the analysis of measures across the entire spectra.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the heterogeneity across different frequency bands' as a strength, indicating different frequency components reflect different neural computations. The frequency-specific nature of selectivity is accepted as a key contribution.

results.result: Low-frequency neural activity better encodes acoustic features (peakRates) than high-frequency amplitude across the cortex, with encoding extending beyond auditory regions to motor and inferior frontal areas. The peakRate & LF model captured the most channels and yielded similar TRF shapes and prediction accuracy (up to 0.55) for both speech and music.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these encoding findings. Reviewer 3 notes the study uses 'encoding models to predict neural responses...and find stronger encoding for both in the low frequency neural responses.' Reviewer 1 acknowledges the 'temporal response function calculation' as straightforward and well-presented. The finding that low-frequency activity better encodes acoustic features is not challenged by any reviewer.

results.result: Connectivity analysis revealed that the auditory cortex connects to the rest of the brain primarily through slow neural dynamics (~33% of channels at delta rate vs. ~12% at HFa). Approximately 70% of significant connections are shared between speech and music, with preferred (~15%) and selective (~12%) connections also present across all frequency bands.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the connectivity findings. Reviewer 3 states the study uses 'pair-wise connectivity (coherence) in order to repeat the shared/selective/preferred analysis across the spectra, suggesting low selectivity.' The comprehensive connectivity analysis across frequency bands is praised, and no reviewer challenges these quantitative findings or their interpretation.

results.result: The study proposes that domain-selective brain regions should be considered as functionally homogeneous but spatially distributed voxels rather than anatomical landmarks, and demonstrates the value of considering shared, preferred, and selective responses across activation/deactivation patterns, frequency bands, and power/connectivity approaches.
results.evaluation: Reviewers have mixed views on this conceptual framework. Reviewer 3 states 'the framework of selective, preferred, and shared is a welcome lens through which to investigate cortical function.' However, Reviewer 1 critiques that 'the authors' categorization...essentially resembles a traditional ANOVA test with posthoc analysis' and warns 'the narrative could potentially lead to an overgeneralized interpretation.' Reviewer 2 notes the categorical approach 'may not fully capture the complexity' and suggests continuous metrics would be more informative.

results.result: The study acknowledges that ecological auditory stimuli are more prone to elicit distributed and dynamical neural responses than shorter stimuli, but also notes that the analytical approach does not allow direct isolation of specific brain operations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly discuss this limitation. Reviewer 1 notes the study 'failed to differentiate between neural responses to the diverse content or local structures within speech and music' and that it 'does not delve into the functional mechanisms.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes 'the study's main approach...may overlook intricate details in neural coding' and that 'speech and music are not entirely orthogonal at different levels of analysis.' The authors' acknowledgment of this limitation is consistent with reviewer concerns.

results.result: The study involved 18 French-speaking epilepsy patients with intact language and hearing functions, using approximately 10 minutes each of natural speech (storytelling) and instrumental music, with extensive cortical coverage (271 electrodes, 3371 contacts).
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently praise the methodological approach. Reviewer 1 highlights 'high-quality sEEG data from a substantial number of patients, covering a majority of brain regions' and 'extensive cortical coverage.' Reviewer 2 notes 'a relatively large corpus of intracranial EEG data' and 'the use of continuous speech and music enhances ecological validity.' Reviewer 3 emphasizes 'important spatial and temporal resolution' and that 'analysis on the level of patient population...supports the generalizability.'

results.result: Data preprocessing included bipolar re-referencing, removal of channels outside the brain (3%), artifact rejection (18% of channels), and analysis across six canonical frequency bands from delta (1-4 Hz) to HFa (80-120 Hz).
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the methodological rigor. Reviewer 3 states 'the statistics and methods employed are rigorous and reliable, estimated based on permutation approaches and cross-validation/regularization was employed and reported properly.' The comprehensive frequency analysis is specifically praised by multiple reviewers as a strength distinguishing this study from prior work.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on methodological quality and study design (C1, C76-C87). Both evaluations praise the high-quality sEEG data, extensive cortical coverage, large patient sample, and ecological validity of continuous stimuli. OpenEval notes internal consistency and proper ethical approval; peer reviewers emphasize spatial/temporal resolution and generalizability.

Complete agreement on preprocessing methods (C88-C92). Both evaluations affirm the appropriateness and rigor of standard preprocessing procedures, artifact rejection, and frequency band selection. Peer reviewers specifically praise permutation approaches and cross-validation/regularization.

Strong agreement on shared neural responses (C2, C16-C20, C22). Both evaluations support the core finding that speech and music largely share network-level brain activities. OpenEval emphasizes convergence across spectral power and connectivity analyses; peer reviewers provide explicit affirmation from all three reviewers. OpenEval also includes C23-C24 and C40-C43, C69 which peer R1 addresses partially (C23-C24) and peer R5 addresses partially (C40-C43).

Significant disagreement on anatomical selectivity claims (C3, C48, C49, C56, C72). OpenEval finds these claims fully supported by population prevalence analyses. However, peer reviewers rate this as UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about theoretical accuracy of selectivity concept, spatial resolution limitations (electrodes record from thousands of neurons), and potential for microscale selectivity being masked.

Strong agreement on frequency-specific selectivity (C4, C25-C27, C44-C47, C62, C73). Both evaluations support that selectivity exists at the level of frequency-specific distributed networks rather than anatomical regions. Peer reviewers praise the comprehensive spectral analysis and acknowledge heterogeneity across frequency bands as a key strength. OpenEval also includes C57 which peer R6 addresses.

Complete agreement on TRF encoding findings (C28-C37, C65-C68). Both evaluations support that low-frequency activity better encodes acoustic features than high-frequency amplitude. Peer reviewers acknowledge the encoding models and temporal response functions as well-presented and straightforward, with no challenges to the quantitative findings.

Complete agreement on connectivity findings (C38-C39). Both evaluations support the seed-based connectivity analysis showing quantitative differences across frequency bands. OpenEval addresses C38-C39 specifically; peer R5 addresses these plus C40-C43 (which OpenEval R2 also covers), affirming low selectivity across spectral signatures in connectivity measures.

Partial disagreement on conceptual framework (C58, C70-C71, C74-C75). OpenEval finds the tripartite classification (shared/preferred/selective) well-supported and valuable. Peer reviewers are UNCERTAIN: one praises it as a 'welcome lens,' but others critique it as resembling traditional ANOVA, potentially oversimplified, and not fully capturing complexity. Suggestion for continuous metrics instead of categorical approach.

Agreement on methodological limitations (C61, C64, C63). Both evaluations acknowledge that the temporal integration approach cannot isolate specific operations and may overlook intricate details in neural coding. OpenEval praises the authors' scientific rigor in acknowledging this; peer reviewers explicitly note the study doesn't differentiate diverse content within speech/music or delve into functional mechanisms.

Agreement on complementary frequency patterns (C23-C24). OpenEval finds these claims supported by Figures 2 and 3, describing frequency-specific patterns. Peer R1 includes these claims in their broader affirmation of shared neural responses, though doesn't specifically discuss the complementary pattern observation.

OpenEval acknowledges sampling bias (C21) and finds the authors appropriately cautious, with evidence that patterns remain similar across hemispheres. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this limitation.

OpenEval finds literature review claims (C5-C15, C50-C55, C59-C60, C63) well-supported with appropriate citations and fair characterization of mixed evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses the literature review, though peer R7 touches on C63 regarding limitations.
